overview.h1: HTS Chapter 78: Lead and Articles Thereof — 2026 Tariff Rates

seo.title: HTS Chapter 78 Lead Tariffs: Refined Lead, Lead Scrap & Lead Sheet HS Codes and Import Duties | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Searchable U.S. duty table for all 13 HTS Chapter 78 lead lines: unwrought lead pays 2.5% on the value of its lead content, plus 10% to 12.5% Section 301 for most countries; USMCA lead from Canada and Mexico is Free; Section 232 does not apply.

overview.intro:
Chapter 78 covers lead: **unwrought lead** (refined lead ingots, antimonial lead, lead bullion and alloys, 7801), **lead waste and scrap** (7802), lead **sheet, strip, foil and powders** (7804) and **other articles of lead** such as wire, pipe and weights (7806). It has 13 tariff lines. Lead ores are Chapter 26, lead oxides Chapter 28, and lead-acid batteries and whole spent batteries Chapter 85.

Base rates are low. All unwrought lead pays **2.5% on the value of the lead content**: the importer declares what the lead in the shipment is worth, and the 2.5% applies to that value only, not to silver or other metals in it. Scrap and powders are Free; sheet, foil and articles pay 1.2% to 3%. USMCA and the other FTAs make every line Free.

Since July 24, 2026 the extra duty that matters is the **2026 Section 301 tariff**: 10% or 12.5% for 60 economies, charged on the full customs value. No Chapter 78 line is on its exemption list. USMCA goods of Canada and Mexico are exempt, and South Korea, Japan and the EU pay a flat 12.5% or 10% in place of the base rate. China pays 12.5% plus 25% (List 3) on 10 lines; Chinese refined lead and scrap are on no China list. **Section 232 does not reach lead**: the metals duties cover steel, aluminum and copper only. Canada's Section 338 duty applied to Canadian refined lead for three weeks (August 22 to September 14, 2026) and then ended. No antidumping or countervailing duty order covers Chapter 78 goods.

workedExamples.title: $10,000 of refined lead from Kazakhstan, $9,000 of it lead
workedExamples.body: The base rate is **2.5% on the value of the lead content**, so the importer declares the lead's value: 2.5% × $9,000 = **$225**, not $250. Kazakhstan's 2026 Section 301 duty (9903.05.51, +12.5%) is charged on the full $10,000 customs value: **$1,250**. Total **$1,475**, about 14.8% of the value.

workedExamples.title: Refined lead from Canada with a USMCA certification
workedExamples.body: USMCA makes the base rate **Free**, and heading 9903.05.93 removes Canada's 10% Section 301 duty for USMCA goods: **$0**. From August 22 to September 14, 2026, Canadian refined lead also paid Canada's **50% Section 338 duty** (9903.03.14), which a USMCA claim did not remove; Proclamation 11065 took refined lead off that list from September 15, 2026. Without a USMCA claim it now pays 2.5% of the lead content plus 10% of the value.

workedExamples.title: Refined lead from South Korea or Australia, $100,000
workedExamples.body: **South Korea:** heading 9903.05.71 charges **12.5% in place of the base rate** when the base rate is lower, so the total is **$12,500** whether or not KORUS is claimed. **Australia:** the U.S.–Australia FTA (AU) makes the base rate Free, and the 2026 Section 301 duty adds **12.5%** (9903.05.23): also **$12,500**.

workedExamples.title: Battery lead scrap from Mexico
workedExamples.body: Lead scrap is Free, but it is not on the 2026 Section 301 exemption list, so non-USMCA scrap from Mexico pays **+10%** (9903.05.55). With a USMCA claim (9903.05.94) it pays **nothing**. Whole spent lead-acid batteries are 8549.11.10, not this line, and their import needs EPA hazardous-waste paperwork.

workedExamples.title: Lead sheet from China
workedExamples.body: 3% base **+ 25%** Section 301 List 3 (9903.88.03) **+ 12.5%** 2026 Section 301 (9903.05.31) = **40.5%**: $40,500 on $100,000. Chinese refined lead (7801.10) is on no China list and pays only 2.5% of its lead content plus 12.5%.

workedExamples.title: Lead bullion containing silver, from Mexico without USMCA
workedExamples.body: A $100,000 lot of bullion whose lead is worth $40,000 (the rest is silver and other metals) pays 2.5% × $40,000 = **$1,000** base duty, plus 10% Section 301 (9903.05.55) on the full $100,000 = **$10,000**. An assay that values the lead correctly keeps the base duty on the lead only.

notes.chapterNotes:
Chapter 78 has no chapter notes of its own; Section XV's notes apply.

**Subheading note 1.** *Refined lead* is metal containing by weight at least 99.9% lead, provided no other element exceeds its limit in the note's table (for example silver 0.02%, arsenic 0.005%, bismuth 0.05%, copper 0.08%, antimony 0.005%, tin 0.005%, zinc 0.002%; other elements 0.001% each).
notes.additionalUsNotes:
Chapter 78 has no additional U.S. notes.

**Statistical note 1.** *Alloys of lead* are metals in which the lead content is, by weight, less than 99% but not less than any other metallic element. Unwrought lead and scrap lines (7801.91, 7801.99, 7802) are reported in kilograms and in kilograms of lead content (Pb kg).

tariffUpdates.h1: HTS Chapter 78 Tariff Updates: Lead Tariffs 2025–2026

seo.title: Lead Tariff Updates 2026: Section 301, USMCA, South Korea, China, Canada Section 338 (HTS Ch. 78) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Every change to U.S. tariffs on lead (HTS Chapter 78) since January 2025, with official sources: the 2026 Section 301 duties, the end of the IEEPA and Section 122 tariffs, Canada's three-week Section 338 duty on refined lead, China List 3 and Russia.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule, the **2025 Basic Edition** (in force January 1, 2025) and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026), and lists every extra duty that reaches Chapter 78 today. Base rates did not change: all 13 lines carry the same general rate in both editions, including **2.5% on the value of the lead content** for unwrought lead.

The extra duties changed three times. In 2025 lead paid the IEEPA tariffs: the reciprocal tariff (lead was not on its exemption list) and the Canada, Mexico and China duties. They ended on **February 24, 2026**, and the 10% **Section 122** surcharge applied until July 23, 2026. Since **July 24, 2026** the **2026 Section 301** tariffs charge every Chapter 78 line at 10% or 12.5% for 60 economies, with USMCA goods exempt. **Section 232 does not cover lead**, and the Section 232 action on processed critical minerals (lead was added to the critical minerals list in November 2025) led to negotiations, not a tariff. Canada's **Section 338** duty reached Canadian refined lead from August 22 to September 14, 2026. China's 25% List 3 duty and Russia's 70% rate stack on top.
tariffUpdates.scope: Chapter 99 measures that reach Chapter 78 from any country: the 2026 Section 301 actions on 60 economies and on Brazil (notes 50, 52), China Section 301 (note 20), Russia's rates in lieu of column 2 (note 30), Canada's Section 338 duty (note 51), the scheduled Nicaragua Section 301 duty (note 29), and the ended IEEPA and Section 122 duties. Section 232 (notes 16, 33, 38 and others) covers no Chapter 78 line, and no antidumping or countervailing duty order covers Chapter 78 goods. For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

changes.title: No Chapter 78 base-rate changes
changes.detail: All 13 Chapter 78 lines carry the same general rate in the 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition; none changed and none are new or renumbered.

changes.title: China Section 301 duties continue during the review
changes.detail: USTR announced that the 2018–2019 Section 301 actions on China, including List 3 (25%) on 10 Chapter 78 lines, continue while the statutory four-year review proceeds.

changes.title: Canadian refined lead taken off the Section 338 list
changes.detail: Proclamation 11065 modified the Section 338 product lists from September 15, 2026 and removed refined lead (7801.10) from the list under 9903.03.14. Canadian refined lead is back to its base rate (Free with USMCA) and, without USMCA, the 10% Section 301 duty.

changes.title: 50% Section 338 duty on Canadian refined lead
changes.detail: Proclamation 11048 imposed 50% (9903.03.14, U.S. note 51(b)) on listed products of Canada, including refined lead (7801.10), effective August 19, 2026; Proclamation 11056 suspended it for three days, and it took effect August 22. Note 51 applies the duty even to goods claiming USMCA. No other Chapter 78 line was on the lists.

changes.title: 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies reach all of Chapter 78
changes.detail: The 10% or 12.5% duties on goods of 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84) took effect. No Chapter 78 line is on the general exemption list (note 52(b)), and lead is not a Section 232 good, so all 13 lines pay. USMCA goods of Canada and Mexico are exempt (9903.05.93, .94). South Korea and Japan pay 12.5%, and the EU 10%, in place of the base rate when it is lower.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 10% Section 122 surcharge (9903.03.01) ended after its 150 days on July 23, 2026; the 2026 Section 301 tariffs took over the next day.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on Brazil
changes.detail: The 25% duty on goods of Brazil (9903.05.01) took effect. No Chapter 78 line is on its exemption list (note 50(a)(ii)), so it stacks with the 12.5% 2026 duty.

changes.title: USMCA joint review: not renewed, still in force
changes.detail: The United States did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form. USTR said the Agreement remains in force pending resolution of the issues or until termination, so USMCA claims (SPI S) still make Canadian and Mexican lead Free and lift the 2026 Section 301 duty.

changes.title: USTR asks for comments on a critical-minerals trade agreement
changes.detail: Following Proclamation 11001, USTR requested public comments on the design of a plurilateral agreement on trade in critical minerals. No tariff on lead has resulted.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs
changes.detail: A 10% surcharge on products of all countries (9903.03.01) applied until July 23, 2026. Chapter 78 was not on its exemption list (9903.03.03), so lead paid it; USMCA goods of Canada and Mexico were exempt.

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China, Brazil and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them for goods entered from 12:00 a.m. ET on February 24.

changes.title: Section 232 on processed critical minerals: negotiations, no tariff
changes.detail: Proclamation 11001 agreed with Commerce that imports of processed critical minerals and their derivative products threaten national security, but directed negotiations with trading partners instead of imposing tariffs. No Section 232 duty applies to lead.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on Nicaragua phases in from 2027
changes.detail: Products of Nicaragua that are not CAFTA-DR originating goods will pay +10% from January 1, 2027 and +15% from January 1, 2028 (9903.89.01, U.S. note 29). The rate is 0% in 2026. It would reach all 13 Chapter 78 lines.

changes.title: China IEEPA fentanyl duty cut to 10%
changes.detail: Executive Order 14357 lowered the IEEPA duty on products of China from 20% to 10% from November 10, 2025. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Lead added to the U.S. critical minerals list
changes.detail: The USGS final 2025 List of Critical Minerals (60 minerals) added lead, along with copper, silver, potash, silicon, rhenium and others. The listing carries no tariff by itself.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff raised to country-specific rates
changes.detail: Executive Order 14326 replaced the 10% baseline with country rates for goods entered from August 7, 2025, for example 15% for Japan and South Korea and 15% in total for the EU. Lead was not exempt. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Extra 40% IEEPA duty on goods of Brazil
changes.detail: Executive Order 14323 added 40% on goods of Brazil, on top of the reciprocal tariff, from August 6, 2025. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Canada IEEPA duty raised to 35% on non-USMCA goods
changes.detail: Raised the IEEPA duty on Canadian goods not entered under USMCA from 25% to 35% (9903.01.10). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff on all Chapter 78 goods
changes.detail: 10% baseline (9903.01.25) on products of all countries except Canada and Mexico, from April 5, 2025. No Chapter 78 line is on the exemption list printed in the schedule (U.S. note 2(v)(iii)), so all lead paid it. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: USMCA goods exempted from the Canada and Mexico duties
changes.detail: From March 7, 2025, goods entered under USMCA were exempt from the IEEPA duties on Canada and Mexico. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: China IEEPA fentanyl duty raised to 20%
changes.detail: Executive Order 14228 raised the IEEPA duty on products of China (9903.01.20) from 10% to 20%, on top of the Section 301 duties. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duties on products of Canada, Mexico and China
changes.detail: +25% on goods of Canada (9903.01.10) and Mexico (9903.01.01), in force from March 4, 2025; +10% on goods of China (9903.01.20) from February 4, 2025. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Russian refined lead: 70% in lieu of column 2
changes.detail: Proclamation 10523 raised the rate on Russian refined and other unwrought lead (7801.10, 7801.99.90; 9903.90.09) from 35% to 70% in place of the column 2 rate.

changes.title: Russian refined lead: 35% in lieu of column 2
changes.detail: Proclamation 10420 set a 35% rate in place of the column 2 rate (9903.90.08) on listed products of Russia, including refined lead (7801.10) and other unwrought lead (7801.99.90).

changes.title: China List 3 raised to 25%
changes.detail: The List 3 duty on 10 Chapter 78 lines (antimonial and other unwrought lead, sheet, foil, powders and other articles), 10% from September 24, 2018, rose to 25%. Refined lead and scrap were never listed.

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of Chapter 78 lead were **$1.27B in 2025**, +29.9% from $976M in 2024 but below the 2022 peak of $1.56B. Almost all of it is unwrought lead: **refined lead (7801.10) was $941M, 74% of the total**, other unwrought lead and alloys (7801.99) $190M and antimonial lead (7801.91) $101M. Sheet, foil and powders (7804) were $12M, other articles (7806) $20M and scrap (7802) only $4M.

**Canada ($445M, +25%) and Mexico ($306M, +101%) supplied 59%**, and USMCA lead from both enters Free. Australia ($187M) and South Korea ($179M, down from $337M in 2023) came next, then the United Kingdom ($53M), Kazakhstan and Ghana. Nigeria fell from $82M in 2024 to $7M, and China from $167M in 2022 to $2M. Germany ships mainly sheet and foil.

2025 is the latest full year of U.S. trade data; the 2026 Section 301 duties (from July 24, 2026) are not yet reflected. Lead ores and concentrates (Chapter 26) and lead-acid batteries (Chapter 85) are not included. Duty-collected figures aren't available from an official source yet.

seo.shortDescription: The total U.S. tariff on lead by country and product: Free for USMCA lead from Canada and Mexico, 12.5% for South Korea and Australia, 10% plus the base rate for the UK, up to 40.5% for China. Lead-content rates, AGOA and FTA claims explained.

industryAreas.intro:
Each cell is the base rate for that product group plus the extra duties for that country, minus any preference, from the current tariff schedule. For lead the 2026 Section 301 tariff sets most of the cost: **10% or 12.5%** on the full value for 60 economies, with no Chapter 78 line exempt. **USMCA** lead from Canada and Mexico pays **nothing**; South Korea and Japan pay a flat **12.5%** and the EU **10%**; Australia pays 12.5% (its FTA removes only the base rate); China pays up to **40.5%** with List 3.

Unwrought lead cells show the base rate as "2.5% on the value of the lead content" because it depends on what the lead in the shipment is worth, which the importer declares; the extra duties are on the full value. Ghana is not one of the 2026 Section 301 economies, so AGOA-qualifying Ghanaian lead is Free. No Section 232 or AD/CVD duty applies to Chapter 78.

assumptions: Each total was computed by the official-measures calculator engine (the same data as the tariff calculator: measures.json, HTSUS 2026 Revision 21) for goods entered on 2026-10-13, priced on a $10,000 shipment and 1,000 units for per-unit rates.
Ranges like "Free · 11.8%" mean the group has lines with different base rates; select a cell to see which lines carry which rate.

Preferences: USMCA (S) is applied for Canada and Mexico on the "USMCA-qualifying" side; AU for Australia; D for Ghana; D for South Africa; D for Nigeria. GSP (A, A+) has lapsed and is not applied. Other preferences are not applied.
Any other country shows the range across every country not listed (column 2 countries — Cuba, North Korea, Russia, Belarus — aside), without preferences.

Unwrought lead (7801) carries a base rate of 2.5% on the value of the lead content. Cells keep that wording because the base duty depends on the lead value the importer declares; the tariff calculator asks for it. Extra duties are charged on the full customs value.

The IEEPA duties (9903.01.xx, 9903.02.xx) are still printed in the schedule but ended February 24, 2026, and the Section 122 surcharge (9903.03.01) expired July 23, 2026; neither is applied. Canada's Section 338 duty on refined lead (9903.03.14) applied August 22 to September 14, 2026 only.
No Section 232 duty reaches Chapter 78, and no antidumping or countervailing duty order covers Chapter 78 goods.
Imports of spent lead-acid batteries and other hazardous waste need EPA notice and consent (40 CFR part 262, subpart H); this is an entry condition, not a duty, and is not shown in the cells.
industryAreas.exemptionCheck: Read U.S. notes 2, 16, 20, 29, 30, 31, 50, 51 and 52 to Chapter 99 subchapter III in the 2026 Revision 21. No Chapter 78 line is on the note 52(b) general exemption list, the note 52(j) country exception lists or the note 50(a)(ii) Brazil list, so the 2026 Section 301 duties reach all 13 lines. No Chapter 78 line is on the Section 232 lists of note 16 (steel, aluminum, copper) or the vehicle and parts notes. China List 3 (note 20(f)) names 7801.91, 7801.99.30, 7801.99.90, 7804.11, 7804.19, 7804.20, 7806.00.03, 7806.00.05 and 7806.00.80; refined lead and scrap are on no list, and note 31 names no Chapter 78 line. Note 30(d) (9903.90.09) names 7801.10 and 7801.99.90. The current note 51(b) Section 338 lists contain no Chapter 78 line; 7801.10 was on the 9903.03.14 list from August 22 to September 14, 2026. The reciprocal (note 2(v)(iii)) and Section 122 (9903.03.03) exemption lists, both ended, named no Chapter 78 line.

tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 78: Lead and Articles Thereof — Import Documents & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Lead: Lead Content Declaration, EPA Rules for Lead Scrap and Spent Batteries, USMCA & Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 78) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: The rules for each HTS Chapter 78 lead line: declaring the lead content for the 2.5% rate, EPA hazardous-waste import notices for spent lead-acid batteries (40 CFR 262 subpart H), the scrap metal exemption, TSCA certification and marking, plus the legal ways to pay less: USMCA, FTAs and AGOA, origin and classification.
keywords: spent lead acid batteries hazardous waste

tariffEngineering.intro:
For lead, two things decide the cost: the **lead content** of unwrought lead, which sets the 2.5% base duty, and the **origin**, which sets the 2026 Section 301 duty (Free for USMCA goods, 10% or 12.5% for most others, up to 37.5% plus the base rate for China). The importer declares the value of the lead in each 7801 shipment, backed by an assay; extra duties are always on the full customs value.

Entry rules come from EPA as much as CBP. **Spent lead-acid batteries** and other hazardous waste can be imported only with EPA notice and consent under **40 CFR part 262, subpart H**, filed through EPA's Waste Import Export Tracking System. Lead **scrap metal** being recycled is exempt from those hazardous-waste rules. Bulk lead needs a TSCA import certification. Each rule and lever links to its regulation.

levers.title: Claim USMCA for Canadian and Mexican lead
levers.saves: The base rate (2.5% of the lead content, up to 3% on articles) and the 10% 2026 Section 301 duty: Canadian or Mexican lead enters Free
levers.appliesTo: All 13 lines, for goods of Canada or Mexico that meet the USMCA rules of origin
levers.document: A USMCA certification of origin (19 CFR 182.12) kept on file, and SPI S on the entry; 9903.05.93 (Canada) or 9903.05.94 (Mexico) lifts the Section 301 duty.
levers.caveat: Lead refined in Canada or Mexico from imported concentrate or scrap must meet the product-specific rule. A USMCA claim did not lift Canada's Section 338 duty on refined lead while it applied (August 22 to September 14, 2026).

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52

levers.title: Claim an FTA or AGOA for the base rate
levers.saves: The base rate only: 2.5% of the lead content on unwrought lead, 1.2% to 3% on sheet, foil and articles
levers.appliesTo: Originating goods of Australia (AU), Chile, Colombia, Peru, Korea (KR) and other FTA partners; AGOA (D) goods of Ghana, Nigeria, South Africa and other general note 16 countries
levers.document: The agreement's proof of origin, or for AGOA the 35% value-content records of general note 16(b), kept on file.
levers.caveat: Except for Ghana and other countries outside the 2026 Section 301 action, the 10% or 12.5% duty still applies. For Korea, Japan and the EU the Section 301 rate replaces the base rate, so an FTA claim changes nothing. AGOA runs through December 31, 2026.

levers.title: Value the lead content correctly
levers.saves: Base duty on the non-lead part: the 2.5% applies to the value of the lead content, not to silver, antimony or other metals
levers.appliesTo: Unwrought lead (7801): refined lead, antimonial lead, lead bullion and alloys
levers.document: An assay or mill certificate showing the lead content (the HTS also asks for the quantity in kg of lead, Pb kg, on 7801.91 and 7801.99) and an invoice that values the lead.
levers.caveat: Only the base duty is on the lead content. Section 301 and all other extra duties are on the full customs value.

levers.title: Avoid Chinese origin for listed lead products
levers.saves: 25% of value on 10 lines: Chinese antimonial lead, sheet, foil, powders and articles pay List 3 on top of 12.5%
levers.appliesTo: 7801.91, 7801.99, 7804 and 7806 goods of China (refined lead and scrap are not listed)
levers.document: Production records showing where the lead was smelted, refined or made. Origin follows the last substantial transformation; ask CBP for a binding ruling if processing happens in more than one country.
levers.caveat: Remelting or simple alloying abroad may not change origin.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 20

levers.title: Classify the lead form correctly
levers.saves: The right base rate: scrap and powders are Free, refined and unwrought lead 2.5% of the lead content, sheet up to 3%
levers.appliesTo: All lines; most often refined vs other unwrought lead (subheading note 1), scrap vs usable lead, and whole spent batteries (8549.11) vs battery scrap (7802)
levers.document: Chemical analysis against the subheading note 1 limits, a description of form and processing, and if unsure a CBP binding ruling.
levers.caveat: Classification follows the product, not the duty. China List 3 and Section 301 rates follow the line, so a wrong class can also change the extra duty.

levers.title: Drawback on exported lead or lead products
levers.saves: Up to 99% of the duties paid on lead that is exported, or used to make exported goods
levers.document: A drawback claim to CBP with import and export records (19 CFR part 191).
levers.caveat: Check with CBP whether a particular Chapter 99 duty is refundable before relying on it.

rules.title: Unwrought lead (7801): base duty of 2.5% on the value of the lead content; declare the lead value and report kilograms and kilograms of lead content (Pb kg) where the HTS asks
2026 Section 301: report the country's 9903.05.xx heading with every Chapter 78 line (no exemption-list line); USMCA goods report 9903.05.93 or 9903.05.94

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52

rules.title: Hazardous waste imports, including spent lead-acid batteries for reclamation: EPA notice and consent through WIETS, a movement document and a contract with the receiving facility
Lead scrap metal being recycled is exempt from the RCRA hazardous-waste rules (excluded scrap metal is excluded altogether); battery-derived materials need a hazardous-waste determination
TSCA import certification for chemical substances in bulk, such as unwrought lead and lead powder; articles need it only if a TSCA rule requires
Country of origin marking; ingots, pigs, plates and sheets are on the J-list, but their outermost container must be marked; scrap and waste are exempt
Russian goods: column 2 rates, 70% in lieu of column 2 on 7801.10 and 7801.99.90 (9903.90.09), plus 12.5% Section 301

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 30

groups.label: Unwrought lead (refined, antimonial, bullion & alloys)
groups.note: 2.5% on the value of the lead content, Free under USMCA and the FTAs; 10% or 12.5% Section 301 on the full value. Chinese refined lead is not on List 3; antimonial and other unwrought lead are. Russian refined lead pays 70%.

groups.label: Lead waste & scrap
groups.note: Free base rate, but 10% or 12.5% Section 301 for non-USMCA goods (no exemption). Lead scrap metal is exempt from RCRA hazardous-waste rules; whole spent batteries (8549.11) are not Chapter 78 and need EPA consent.

groups.label: Lead sheet, strip, foil & powders
groups.note: 2.2% (foil up to 0.2 mm), 3% (thicker sheet) or Free (powders and flakes); China pays 37.5% extra.

groups.label: Other articles of lead
groups.note: 1.2% (bars, rods, wire), 2% (pipes and fittings) or 3% (other articles); China pays 37.5% extra.

tariffEngineering.disclaimer: A checklist of where the rules are, with links to the regulations, not legal advice. Chapter 99 rates change often, and EPA's import rules depend on whether a material is a hazardous waste; check the current Chapter 99 notes, CBP's CSMS messages and EPA's requirements before importing.

seo.title: Lead Tariff FAQ 2026: Is There a Tariff on Lead? Lead Ingot, Scrap & Battery HS Codes, EPA Rules (HTS Ch. 78) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Answers to what people search about U.S. lead imports: the tariff on lead, the lead-content rate, HS codes for lead ingots, alloys, scrap, sheet and batteries, EPA rules for lead scrap and spent batteries, China, critical minerals and import sources.
keywords: is there a tariff on lead

finalConclusion.intro: Straight answers to the most-searched questions about U.S. tariffs and import rules for lead, by product, by country and by HS code. Each answer links to the page with the detail and the official sources.
keyTakeaways: Unwrought lead pays a base rate of 2.5% on the value of its lead content; scrap and powders are Free; sheet, foil and articles 1.2% to 3%. USMCA and the FTAs make every line Free.

The 2026 Section 301 tariff (from July 24, 2026) adds 10% or 12.5% of the full value for 60 economies, with no Chapter 78 line exempt. USMCA lead from Canada and Mexico pays nothing; South Korea and Japan pay a flat 12.5%, the EU 10%; China up to 40.5%.

Section 232 does not cover lead, the critical-minerals Section 232 action produced no tariff, and no AD/CVD order covers Chapter 78. The IEEPA and Section 122 tariffs have ended; Canada's Section 338 duty on refined lead lasted from August 22 to September 14, 2026.

In 2025 the U.S. imported $1.27B of Chapter 78 lead, 74% of it refined lead, 59% from Canada and Mexico. Spent lead-acid batteries need EPA notice and consent to import; lead scrap metal for recycling does not.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on lead?
searchedAs: is there a tariff on lead
faqs.answer: Yes, but it is modest for most suppliers. Unwrought lead (7801) has a base rate of 2.5% on the value of its lead content, scrap and powders are Free, and sheet, foil and articles pay 1.2% to 3%. Since July 24, 2026 the 2026 Section 301 tariff adds 10% or 12.5% of the full value for 60 economies, including South Korea, Australia, the UK, the EU and China; USMCA lead from Canada and Mexico pays nothing. Section 232 does not apply to lead.

faqs.question: What does "2.5% on the value of the lead content" mean?
faqs.answer: It is the base rate on all unwrought lead (refined lead, antimonial lead, bullion and alloys, heading 7801). The 2.5% applies only to the value of the lead in the shipment, which the importer declares from an assay, not to silver or other metals in it: $10,000 of refined lead with $9,000 of lead content pays $225. Extra duties such as Section 301 are charged on the full customs value.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for lead?
faqs.answer: Lead is HS Chapter 78: 7801 unwrought lead (7801.10 refined, 7801.91 antimonial, 7801.99 other, including bullion and alloys), 7802 lead waste and scrap, 7804 plates, sheets, strip, foil, powders and flakes, and 7806 other articles of lead. The U.S. schedule splits these into 13 ten-digit lines. Lead ore is 2607 and lead-acid batteries 8507.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for lead ingots?
faqs.answer: Refined lead ingots and pigs (at least 99.9% lead, within the subheading note 1 limits) are 7801.10.00.00. Lead bullion is 7801.99.30.00, and other unwrought lead, including remelted lead that is not refined, is 7801.99.90. All pay 2.5% on the value of the lead content, Free under USMCA and the FTAs.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for antimonial lead and lead alloys?
faqs.answer: Unwrought lead containing antimony as the principal other element (antimonial lead) is 7801.91.00.00; other lead alloys are 7801.99.90.30. Both pay 2.5% on the value of the lead content. Unlike refined lead, both are on China's Section 301 List 3, so Chinese antimonial lead pays 25% plus 12.5% on top.

faqs.question: What is the HS code and tariff for lead scrap?
searchedAs: lead waste and scrap hs code
lead acid battery scrap hs code
faqs.answer: Lead waste and scrap is 7802.00.00: .30 for scrap obtained from lead-acid storage batteries, .60 for other scrap. The base rate is Free, but the 2026 Section 301 duty (10% or 12.5%) applies to non-USMCA scrap. Whole spent lead-acid batteries are classified in 8549.11 (8549.11.10 for recovery of lead, Free), not in Chapter 78.

faqs.question: What is the HS code and duty for lead-acid batteries?
searchedAs: lead acid battery import duty rate
faqs.answer: New lead-acid batteries are Chapter 85, not Chapter 78: 8507.10.00 for starter batteries and 8507.20.80 for other lead-acid batteries, both 3.5% base. Spent batteries for lead recovery are 8549.11.10 (Free). Chapter 99 duties for those lines are covered on the Chapter 85 pages.

faqs.question: Do you need a license to import lead scrap or used lead-acid batteries?
searchedAs: used lead-acid batteries can be shipped across international
used lead acid batteries shipped across international borders
faqs.answer: There is no U.S. import license for lead, but spent lead-acid batteries imported for reclamation are hazardous waste: the importer or foreign exporter must give EPA notice and get consent through EPA's Waste Import Export Tracking System, with a movement document and a contract with the receiving facility (40 CFR 262.84, 266.80). Lead scrap metal being recycled is exempt from those rules (40 CFR 261.6(a)(3)(ii)).

faqs.question: Are spent lead-acid batteries exempt from hazardous waste rules?
searchedAs: spent lead acid batteries are exempt from hazardous waste
spent lead acid batteries are exempt from hazardous waste regulations
faqs.answer: Partly. Under 40 CFR 266.80, people who collect, transport or store spent lead-acid batteries for reclamation are exempt from most hazardous-waste requirements, or can manage them as universal waste (40 CFR part 273). Importers are not fully exempt: imports must follow 40 CFR part 262, subpart H (notice, consent and movement documents), and reclaimers that store batteries must meet 266.80(b).

faqs.question: What is the HS code for lead sheet and foil?
faqs.answer: Lead sheets, strip and foil up to 0.2 mm thick (excluding any backing) are 7804.11.00.00 at 2.2%; thicker plates and sheets are 7804.19.00.00 at 3%; lead powders and flakes 7804.20.00.00, Free. Chinese lead sheet pays 40.5% in total.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for lead wire, pipe and weights?
faqs.answer: Lead bars, rods, profiles and wire are 7806.00.03.00 (1.2%); lead tubes, pipes and fittings 7806.00.05.00 (2%); other articles of lead, such as weights, 7806.00.80.00 (3%). Lead powder is 7804.20.00.00 (Free). Articles made for a specific use elsewhere in the schedule are classified there instead.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on lead products from China?
faqs.answer: Chinese lead pays the 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty on every line. Antimonial and other unwrought lead, sheet, foil, powders and articles (10 lines) also pay 25% under List 3: for example 40.5% in total on lead sheet. Chinese refined lead (7801.10) and scrap (7802) are on no China list and pay 12.5% plus the base rate.

faqs.question: Is lead a critical mineral, and does that bring a tariff?
searchedAs: is lead on the critical minerals list
are zinc and lead critical minerals
faqs.answer: Yes, lead is on the U.S. critical minerals list: the USGS final 2025 list (November 7, 2025) added it. That does not bring a tariff by itself. The Section 232 action on processed critical minerals (Proclamation 11001, January 14, 2026) chose negotiations instead of duties, and the Section 232 metals duties cover only steel, aluminum and copper.

faqs.question: Where does the U.S. get its lead from?
searchedAs: where does the us get lead from
faqs.answer: In 2025 the U.S. imported $1.27B of Chapter 78 lead products, 74% of it refined lead. The largest suppliers were Canada $445M, Mexico $306M, Australia $187M, South Korea $179M, United Kingdom $53M. Canada and Mexico together supplied 59%. Lead ores (Chapter 26) are not included.
